concepts.name: The five standard answer choices
concepts.description: Every Data Sufficiency question uses the same five options, describing every possible combination of sufficiency.

concepts.name: One statement alone is sufficient
concepts.description: A statement is sufficient by itself if it pins down exactly one possible answer to the question.

concepts.name: Sufficient only when combined
concepts.description: Sometimes neither statement alone narrows things down enough, but using both together does.

concepts.name: Not sufficient even together
concepts.description: If more than one answer is still possible after using both statements, the data is not sufficient.

concepts.name: Testing each statement independently
concepts.description: Always test statement (1) alone and statement (2) alone — completely separately — before ever considering them together.

formulas.title: The five standard options
formulas.prompt: What are the five standard Data Sufficiency answer choices?
formulas.formula:
A: (1) alone is sufficient, (2) alone is not.
B: (2) alone is sufficient, (1) alone is not.
C: Both together are sufficient, but neither alone.
D: Each statement alone is sufficient.
E: Not sufficient even together.
formulas.explanation: These five options cover every possible outcome, so exactly one of them is always correct.
formulas.example: If statement (1) alone answers the question but statement (2) alone does not, the answer is A.
formulas.commonMistake: Confusing option A with option D, or option C with option E.
formulas.applicationPrompt: What does option C mean in a Data Sufficiency question?

formulas.title: Test each statement separately first
formulas.prompt: What is the standard strategy for approaching a Data Sufficiency question?
formulas.formula:
Test statement (1) alone (forgetting statement (2) completely).
Then test statement (2) alone (forgetting statement (1) completely).
Only combine them if neither alone works.
formulas.explanation: Testing them in this fixed order avoids the common trap of assuming information from one statement while testing the other.
formulas.example: Even if statement (2) looks obviously useful, still test statement (1) alone, in isolation, first.
formulas.commonMistake: Combining the statements immediately without checking each one alone first.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Why should you test statement (1) in complete isolation from statement (2)?

formulas.title: Recognising sufficiency
formulas.prompt: When is a single statement "sufficient" on its own?
formulas.formula: A statement is sufficient if it leads to exactly one possible value or answer, and insufficient if more than one value remains possible
formulas.explanation: The statement does not need to be a full equation — it just needs to leave no ambiguity in the final answer.
formulas.example: "x is divisible by 6" is sufficient to answer "is x even?" because every multiple of 6 is even
formulas.commonMistake: Assuming a statement is insufficient just because it does not directly give a numeric value.
formulas.applicationPrompt: Is "x is divisible by 6" sufficient to answer "is x even?"

formulas.title: Combining statements
formulas.prompt: How do you know when to combine both statements?
formulas.formula: If both statement (1) alone and statement (2) alone leave more than one possibility, combine them and see if only one possibility survives
formulas.explanation: Combining rules out possibilities allowed by one statement but excluded by the other.
formulas.example: (1) x+y=10 alone: infinitely many pairs. (2) x−y=4 alone: also infinitely many pairs. Together: a unique solution, x=7,y=3
formulas.commonMistake: Giving up and calling the data insufficient without actually testing the combination.
formulas.applicationPrompt: If x+y=10 and x−y=4 are given as two separate statements, what happens when they are combined?

formulas.title: Recognising true insufficiency
formulas.prompt: How do you confirm that even both statements together are not sufficient?
formulas.formula: Find at least two different values that satisfy both statements at once but give different answers to the question
formulas.explanation: A single counterexample pair is enough to prove that the combined data is not sufficient.
formulas.example: (1) x > 5 and (2) x < 10 together only give a range, 5 < x < 10, which still allows many different values of x
formulas.commonMistake: Assuming that combining two statements must always narrow things down to one answer.
formulas.applicationPrompt: If x > 5 and x < 10 are the only two statements given, is that enough to find the exact value of x?

formulas.title: A definite "No" is sufficient
formulas.prompt: In a yes/no data sufficiency question, when is a statement sufficient?
formulas.formula:
Sufficient = always the same answer, Yes or No
Insufficient = Yes for some values, No for others
formulas.explanation: The question asks whether the answer can be determined, not whether it is Yes.
formulas.example: Is x > 5? Statement: x < 3. The answer is always No, so the statement is sufficient.
formulas.commonMistake: Marking a statement insufficient because it answers "No".
formulas.applicationPrompt: Is n even? Statement: n² is odd.

formulas.title: Two equations that are really one
formulas.prompt: Two statements each give an equation in x and y. When are they not enough together?
formulas.formula: Two equations fix two unknowns only if one is not a multiple of the other
formulas.explanation: A multiple of an equation carries no new information.
formulas.example: x + y = 10 and 2x + 2y = 20 together still leave x = 3, y = 7 or x = 4, y = 6: not sufficient.
formulas.commonMistake: Counting equations without checking that they are independent.

levels.title: Five Options, One Strategy
levels.description: Every Data Sufficiency question is answered the same way: test each statement alone, then combine only if needed.

blocks.title: The same five answers, every time
blocks.body: A Data Sufficiency question never asks you to actually solve the problem — only to decide whether it CAN be solved, and with which information. There are always exactly five possible answers, covering every combination of "alone" and "together."

blocks.title: The five options
blocks.body: A: (1) alone. B: (2) alone. C: both together, not alone. D: each alone. E: not even together.
blocks.caption: Exactly one of these five is always the correct answer.

blocks.body: Always test statement (1) in total isolation from statement (2), and vice versa, before ever combining them.

levels.title: Data Sufficiency Formulas
levels.description: The five standard options, the testing strategy, recognising single and combined sufficiency, and true insufficiency.

levels.title: Single-Statement Sufficiency
levels.description: Recognising when one statement alone is enough (or each is).

levels.title: Sharper Single Statements and Simple Combinations
levels.description: Trickier single-statement cases, and straightforward combined-sufficiency problems.

levels.title: Harder Combinations and True Insufficiency
levels.description: Using one statement to filter another, and recognising when even both together fail.

questions.question: What is the value of x? (1) x + 5 = 12. (2) x is a positive integer.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone gives x = 7 directly — a single, definite value, so it is sufficient. Statement (2) alone allows countless positive integers, so it is not sufficient alone.
solutionSteps: (1): x + 5 = 12 → x = 7. Sufficient.
(2): many positive integers fit. Not sufficient.
questions.method: Test each statement completely on its own.

hints.text: Solve statement (1) by itself: does it give one definite value?

commonMistakes: Assuming a vague property statement like (2) is enough on its own.

questions.question: In a Data Sufficiency question, option C means

options.text: statement (1) alone is sufficient
both statements together are sufficient, but neither alone is
each statement alone is sufficient
neither statement is sufficient, even together

questions.explanation: Option C specifically means the two statements are only sufficient when combined — neither one works by itself.
solutionSteps: Option C = sufficient together, not sufficient separately.
questions.method: Match the outcome to the exact wording of each option.

hints.text: Option C requires that neither statement works alone.

commonMistakes: Confusing option C with option D (each alone sufficient).

questions.question: What is the value of y? (1) 2y = 16. (2) y > 0.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone gives y = 8, a single definite value — sufficient. Statement (2) alone only says y is positive, which still allows countless values — not sufficient.
solutionSteps: (1): 2y = 16 → y = 8. Sufficient.
(2): y > 0 allows many values. Not sufficient.
questions.method: Check whether each statement alone pins down one exact value.

hints.text: A statement giving an equation is often sufficient by itself.

commonMistakes: Assuming statement (2) alone is enough just because it is true.

questions.question: Is n even? (1) n is divisible by 4. (2) n is divisible by 6.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone: every multiple of 4 is even, so it is sufficient by itself. Statement (2) alone: every multiple of 6 is also even, so it too is sufficient by itself. Since each works alone, the answer is D.
solutionSteps: (1): multiples of 4 are always even. Sufficient.
(2): multiples of 6 are always even. Sufficient.
Each alone works → D.
questions.method: Test each statement completely independently before comparing results.

hints.text: Check whether statement (1) alone is enough, then separately check statement (2) alone.

commonMistakes: Stopping after confirming statement (1) works, without checking statement (2) alone too.

questions.question: What is the value of x? (1) x² = 25. (2) x > 0.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone gives x = 5 or x = −5 — two possibilities, so it is not sufficient alone. Statement (2) alone only says x is positive, allowing countless values — not sufficient alone. Together, only x = 5 satisfies both, so combined they are sufficient.
solutionSteps: (1): x = ±5. Not sufficient.
(2): x > 0 alone allows many values. Not sufficient.
Together: only x = 5 fits both. Sufficient.
questions.method: Test each statement alone first, then combine only if needed.

hints.text: A squared equation usually gives two possible roots.

commonMistakes: Assuming statement (1) alone gives a single answer, forgetting the negative root.

questions.question: Is x > 0? (1) x² > 0. (2) x³ > 0.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone: x² > 0 just means x is not zero — x could be positive or negative, so it is not sufficient. Statement (2) alone: cubing preserves the sign of a number, so x³ > 0 means x must be positive — sufficient by itself.
solutionSteps: (1): x² > 0 allows x positive or negative. Not sufficient.
(2): x³ > 0 forces x > 0. Sufficient.
questions.method: Remember that squaring hides the sign, but cubing preserves it.

hints.text: Squaring a negative number also gives a positive result.

commonMistakes: Assuming statement (1) also proves x is positive, like statement (2) does.

questions.question: What is the average (mean) of 5 numbers? (1) Their sum is 50. (2) Their median is 10.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone: mean = sum ÷ count = 50 ÷ 5 = 10 — a single definite value, sufficient. Statement (2) alone: knowing the median tells you nothing about the sum or mean of the other numbers, so it is not sufficient.
solutionSteps: (1): mean = 50 ÷ 5 = 10. Sufficient.
(2): median does not determine the mean. Not sufficient.
questions.method: Check whether the given statistic actually determines the one you need.

hints.text: The median and the mean are generally independent pieces of information.

commonMistakes: Assuming the median and mean must be equal or related.

questions.question: Is quadrilateral ABCD a square? (1) All four sides are equal. (2) All four angles are equal.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone: equal sides describe a rhombus, which is not necessarily a square. Not sufficient. Statement (2) alone: equal angles describe a rectangle, which is not necessarily a square. Not sufficient. Together: equal sides AND equal angles force a square. Sufficient.
solutionSteps: (1): equal sides → rhombus, not necessarily square. Not sufficient.
(2): equal angles → rectangle, not necessarily square. Not sufficient.
Together: equal sides and angles → square. Sufficient.
questions.method: Think of shapes that satisfy one condition but not the other.

hints.text: A rhombus has equal sides but is not always a square.

commonMistakes: Assuming equal sides alone already guarantees a square.

questions.question: What is the value of x? (1) x + y = 10. (2) x − y = 4.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone: infinitely many (x,y) pairs satisfy x+y=10. Not sufficient. Statement (2) alone: infinitely many pairs satisfy x−y=4 too. Not sufficient. Together: solving the two equations gives a unique x = 7. Sufficient.
solutionSteps: (1) alone: infinitely many pairs. Not sufficient.
(2) alone: infinitely many pairs. Not sufficient.
Together: unique solution x = 7. Sufficient.
questions.method: Two linear equations in two unknowns usually need both to pin down a unique solution.

hints.text: One linear equation in two unknowns never gives a unique answer by itself.

commonMistakes: Assuming one equation is already sufficient because it "looks solvable."

questions.question: Is x a multiple of 3? (1) x is a multiple of 9. (2) x is a multiple of 6.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone: every multiple of 9 is also a multiple of 3. Sufficient. Statement (2) alone: every multiple of 6 is also a multiple of 3. Sufficient. Since each works alone, the answer is D.
solutionSteps: (1): multiples of 9 are always multiples of 3. Sufficient.
(2): multiples of 6 are always multiples of 3. Sufficient.
Each alone works → D.
questions.method: Check whether each divisibility statement alone forces the answer.

hints.text: 9 and 6 are both themselves multiples of 3.

commonMistakes: Assuming you need both statements just because there are two of them.

questions.question: What is the value of x? (1) x² − 5x + 6 = 0. (2) x > 2.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone: factorises to (x−2)(x−3)=0, giving x = 2 or x = 3 — two possibilities, not sufficient. Statement (2) alone: x > 2 allows countless values, not sufficient. Together: of the two roots from (1), only x = 3 satisfies x > 2, so the combination gives a unique answer.
solutionSteps: (1): x = 2 or x = 3. Not sufficient.
(2) alone: x > 2 allows many values. Not sufficient.
Together: only x = 3 satisfies both. Sufficient.
questions.method: Use statement (2) to filter the possibilities left by statement (1).

hints.text: Statement (1) narrows x to a short list; statement (2) can then filter that list.

commonMistakes: Assuming statement (1) is already sufficient because it "solves" the equation.

questions.question: Is the number n prime? (1) n is odd. (2) n has exactly two positive divisors.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone: many odd numbers are not prime (9, 15, 21, …), so it is not sufficient. Statement (2) alone: having exactly two positive divisors is the definition of a prime number, so it is sufficient by itself.
solutionSteps: (1): odd numbers like 9 and 15 are not prime. Not sufficient.
(2): "exactly two divisors" is the definition of prime. Sufficient.
questions.method: Recognise when a statement is actually a definition in disguise.

hints.text: Think of a specific odd composite number as a counterexample for statement (1).

commonMistakes: Assuming all odd numbers are prime.

questions.question: What is the value of x? (1) x > 5. (2) x < 10.

options.text: Statement (1) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (2) alone is not sufficient.
Statement (2) ALONE is sufficient, but statement (1) alone is not sufficient.
BOTH statements TOGETHER are sufficient, but NEITHER statement alone is sufficient.
EACH statement ALONE is sufficient.
Statements (1) and (2) TOGETHER are still NOT sufficient.

questions.explanation: Statement (1) alone allows any value greater than 5 — not sufficient. Statement (2) alone allows any value less than 10 — not sufficient. Even combined, they only narrow x down to the range 5 < x < 10, which still contains infinitely many possible values, so the data is not sufficient even together.
solutionSteps: (1) alone: x > 5, infinitely many values. Not sufficient.
(2) alone: x < 10, infinitely many values. Not sufficient.
Together: 5 < x < 10, still infinitely many values. Not sufficient.
questions.method: A range of possible values, however narrow, is not the same as a single definite answer.

hints.text: Combining a "greater than" and a "less than" statement usually just gives a range, not a single value.

commonMistakes: Assuming that combining any two statements must always produce a unique answer.
